title: Financing a $65k Electric Vehicle on a $75k Salary
planText: I make $75k/year pre-tax. I have $5k saved for a down payment and plan to finance a new $65k electric SUV on a 72-month loan at 6.8% interest (about $1,020/month payment). I justify this because I will save $180/month on gasoline and the car has high safety ratings.

pessimist.headline: A single repair or insurance hike will cause immediate car repossession.

points.claim: EV insurance premiums for high-value vehicles are dramatically higher, wiping out gas savings.
points.suggestedFix: Get insurance quotes from 3 carriers before signing any dealership paperwork.

points.claim: Luxury EVs depreciate by 40-50% in the first three years, putting you deeply underwater.
points.suggestedFix: Buy a 2-year pre-owned EV to let the first owner absorb the initial depreciation curve.

pessimist.verdict: Financial catastrophe waiting to happen on a 72-month subprime amortization.

accountant.headline: Vehicle expenses will swallow 32% of your monthly net income.

points.claim: Net take-home pay on $75k is ~$4,600/mo; car payment ($1,020) + insurance ($250) + electricity ($70) = $1,340/mo.
points.suggestedFix: Follow the 20/4/10 rule: 20% down, 4-year term, payment under 10% of gross ($625/mo max).

points.claim: Over 72 months, you will pay over $14,000 in non-recoverable loan interest alone.
points.suggestedFix: Cap total vehicle purchase price at $35k or lower.

accountant.verdict: Severe violation of sound personal financial planning guidelines.

skepticalParent.headline: A car is not an investment; it is a depreciating asset that locks you into debt.

points.claim: You have only $5k in emergency savings; draining it leaves you with zero safety margin.
points.suggestedFix: Preserve your emergency fund and buy a reliable $15k-$20k vehicle with partial cash.

skepticalParent.verdict: Showing off with a luxury vehicle at the expense of your financial independence is foolish.

futureYou.headline: In 3 years you will hate this car payment as you watch friends buy homes.

points.claim: Car debt directly destroys your debt-to-income (DTI) ratio when applying for a mortgage.
points.suggestedFix: Keep debt payments under 5% of income to preserve future borrowing power.

futureYou.verdict: This single impulsive vehicle purchase sets your wealth accumulation back by half a decade.

optimist.headline: EV technology is the future and the driving experience is unparalleled.

points.claim: Maintenance costs on EVs (brakes, fluids) are demonstrably lower over 5 years.
points.suggestedFix: Capture the EV benefits without the price tag by leasing an affordable EV under $350/mo.

optimist.verdict: Desire for modern EV tech is sensible, but target an entry-level model or lease incentive.

judge.rationale: Allocating nearly a third of net income to a rapidly depreciating luxury vehicle creates extreme financial vulnerability. Re-anchoring to an affordable certified pre-owned or lease structure achieves the safety and fuel benefits without bankrupting the user.
topRisks: Severe monthly cashflow deficit ($1,340/mo car overhead on $4,600/mo net income)
Zero remaining emergency fund after applying $5k down payment
Negative equity trap with 72-month loan on a steep EV depreciation curve
judge.hardenedPlan: Option A (Recommended): Purchase a 2022 Certified Pre-Owned EV or hybrid for $25k-$30k. Put $2,500 down, keeping $2,500 emergency buffer. Finance for 48 months at ~$550/mo. Option B: Take advantage of manufacturer subvented EV leases offering $299-$349/month with $2k down, keeping the rest in savings.

actionItems.task: Obtain written comprehensive insurance quotes for EV vs hybrid vehicles
Calculate exact monthly budget breakdown including rent and living costs
Test drive 2 pre-owned EV models under $30,000

unresolvedQuestions: Do you have home charging capability or will you rely on expensive public superchargers?
What are your medium-term goals for home ownership or graduate school?
